questions.question_text:
Consider the claim $1 + 4 + 7 + \dots + (3n - 2) = \dfrac{n(3n - 1)}{2}$ for all integers $n \ge 1$.
Which line is the correct inductive hypothesis?

options.why: Assumes the result for every $k$ at once, which is the whole statement being proved, so the argument becomes circular.
The last term has been written with $n = k + 1$ substituted, so the left side runs one term further than the right side allows.
Assumes only that the final term equals the closed form, dropping all the earlier terms of the sum.

questions.solution_text:
The hypothesis is the whole statement with $n$ replaced by $k$, assumed for one integer $k$.
$1 + 4 + 7 + \dots + (3k - 2) = \dfrac{k(3k - 1)}{2}$ for some integer $k \ge 1$

questions.question_text:
A proof by induction is required for the claim $2^{n} > 2n$ for all integers $n \ge 3$.
Which statement correctly describes what the base case must verify?

options.why: Tests $n = 1$ when the claim starts at $n = 3$, so the real first case is never checked.
That is the inductive hypothesis; the base case substitutes an actual number, not the letter $k$.
Checking a run of values is not a base case; induction needs one starting value plus the step.

questions.solution_text:
The base case is the smallest value in the claim, $n = 3$.
$LHS = 2^{3} = 8$
$RHS = 2(3) = 6$
$8 > 6$, so the statement is true for $n = 3$.

questions.question_text: For the claim $1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 + \dots + n(n + 1) = \dfrac{1}{3}n(n + 1)(n + 2)$ for all integers $n \ge 1$, which statement must the inductive step prove?

options.why: The added term was formed by substituting $n = k + 2$ instead of $n = k + 1$ into $n(n + 1)$.
Only two of the three factors of the closed form were shifted; the factor $n + 2$ was dropped rather than becoming $k + 3$.
That is the inductive hypothesis, the statement assumed at $n = k$, not the statement to be proved.

questions.solution_text:
Replace every $n$ by $k + 1$, and add the $(k + 1)$th term to the left side.
The added term is $(k + 1)\left((k + 1) + 1\right) = (k + 1)(k + 2)$.
$1 \times 2 + \dots + k(k + 1) + (k + 1)(k + 2) = \dfrac{1}{3}(k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3)$

questions.question_text:
In a proof that $9^{n} + 3$ is divisible by $6$ for all integers $n \ge 1$, a student writes the line $9^{k} + 3 = 6p$, where $p$ is an integer.
What is the role of this line?

options.text: It is the inductive hypothesis: the statement assumed true for one integer $k \ge 1$
It is the base case: the statement checked at the smallest value of $n$
options.why: A base case substitutes a number for $n$ and evaluates both sides; this line keeps the letter $k$.

options.text: It is the statement the inductive step must prove
options.why: The step must prove the $n = k + 1$ version, $9^{k + 1} + 3 = 6q$; this line is what is assumed, not what is shown.

options.text: It is the conclusion of the proof
options.why: The conclusion states the result for all $n$ and comes after the step; this line is written before the step begins.

questions.solution_text:
The line is the claim with $n$ replaced by $k$, written in the divisibility form $6 \times (\text{an integer})$.
It is the inductive hypothesis, assumed for one integer $k \ge 1$.

questions.question_text: Why is assuming the statement true for $n = k$ not circular reasoning?

options.text: Because the step proves only a conditional, that truth at $n = k$ forces truth at $n = k + 1$, while the base case supplies one value where the statement really does hold
Because $k$ is a different letter from $n$, so a different statement is being assumed
options.why: The letter is irrelevant; what saves the argument is that the assumption is used only inside a conditional.

options.text: Because the assumption is checked separately for every integer $k$ before it is used
options.why: No such check happens, and checking every integer is exactly the work induction is designed to avoid.

options.text: Because the base case has already shown the statement is true for every value of $k$
options.why: The base case establishes one value only; it does not establish the statement at a general $k$.

questions.solution_text:
The inductive step never asserts that the statement holds at $n = k$.
It proves the conditional: if the statement holds at $n = k$, then it holds at $n = k + 1$.
The base case gives one integer where the statement genuinely holds, and the conditional then carries that truth to every later integer.

questions.question_text:
The claim $3 + 6 + 12 + \dots + 3(2^{n}) = 3(2^{n + 1} - 1)$ is made for all integers $n \ge 0$.
Which line correctly tests the base case?

options.why: Starts at $n = 1$ when the claim begins at $n = 0$, leaving the first case of the claim unchecked.
Reads the $n = 0$ left side as an empty sum instead of the single term $3 \times 2^{0} = 3$.
Substituted $n = 0$ into $2^{n}$ on the right instead of into $2^{n + 1}$.

questions.solution_text:
The claim starts at $n = 0$, so the base case is $n = 0$.
$LHS = 3 \times 2^{0} = 3$
$RHS = 3(2^{0 + 1} - 1) = 3(2 - 1) = 3$
$LHS = RHS$, so the statement is true for $n = 0$.

questions.question_text:
A proof has verified a claim at $n = 2$ and has shown that its truth at $n = k$ forces its truth at $n = k + 1$ for every integer $k \ge 2$.
Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Since the statement is true for $n = 2$, by mathematical induction it is true for all integers $n \ge 2$
Since the statement is true for $n = 2$, by mathematical induction it is true for all integers $n \ge 1$
options.why: Extends the conclusion below the base case, where nothing has been verified and the step is not available.

options.text: Since the statement is true for $n = 2$, by mathematical induction it is true for all real numbers $n \ge 2$
options.why: Induction steps from one integer to the next, so it establishes nothing about non-integer values.

options.text: Since the statement is true for $n = k$, by mathematical induction it is true for all integers $n \ge 2$
options.why: Cites the assumption as the verified case; it is the base case at $n = 2$ that must be true, not the hypothesis.

questions.solution_text:
The verified case is $n = 2$, and the step carries truth upwards from there.
Since the statement is true for $n = 2$, by mathematical induction it is true for all integers $n \ge 2$.

questions.question_text:
For a statement $P(n)$ it has been shown that $P(k)$ implies $P(k + 1)$ for every integer $k \ge 1$, and that $P(4)$ is true.
Nothing else is known.
Which conclusion is justified?

options.why: The implication only moves upwards, so it says nothing about the integers below the one case known to be true.
Omits $n = 4$ itself, which is the case that has actually been verified.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because the verified case was not $n = 1$
options.why: A base case may sit at any integer; the conclusion then runs from that integer upwards.

questions.solution_text:
$P(4)$ is true, and $P(4)$ implies $P(5)$, which implies $P(6)$, and so on.
The chain starts at $4$ and runs upwards only.
$P(n)$ is true for every integer $n \ge 4$.
